Extinct in Shōwa 34 (1959) |Family Crest = Japanese Crest Ume.svg |Crest Name = {{ruby|Ume|うめ}} |Main Lineage = {{ill|Genji|ja|源氏#花山源氏|lt=Hanayama Genji|lt_ja=花山源氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Genji|1=Minamoto clan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q599881}} {{ill|Legitimate Line|ja|嫡流|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Legitimate Line|1=Legitimate Line|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11447787}} |Founding Ancestor = {{ill|Minamoto Genken|ja|源顕康|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Minamoto Genken|1=minamoto no akiyasu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q118746998}} |Classification = {{ill|Kuge|en|Kuge|WD=Q1196276|lt=Kuge}} ({{ill|Semi‐noble|ja|半家 (公家)|1=Half-house (Kuge)|2=ja|3=半家 (公家)|lt=Semi‐noble|lt_ja=半家|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Semi‐noble|qq=}})
{{ill|Kazoku|en|Kazoku|WD=Q241734|lt=Kazoku}} ({{ill|Viscount|en|Viscount|WD=Q185902|lt=Viscount}}) |Origin = {{ill|Yamashiro Province|ja|Yamashiro Province|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamashiro Province|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} |Base = {{ill|Yamashiro Province|ja|Yamashiro Province|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamashiro Province|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} |Branch = {{ill|Shinagawa Family (Hanayama Genji)|ja|品川氏#品川氏（花山源氏）|lt=Shinagawa Family|lt_ja=品川氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinagawa Family (Hanayama Genji)|1=Shinagawa Family (Hanayama Genji)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11418409}} ({{ill|Samurai|ja|武家|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Samurai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=buke|WD=Q2927809}}) }} '''Shirakawa Hakuou‐ke''' (白川伯王家), also known as '''Shirakawa‐ke''' (白川家), was a family of Japan’s {{ill|Kuge|en|Kuge|WD=Q1196276|lt=Kuge}} and {{ill|Kazoku|en|Kazoku|WD=Q241734|lt=Kazoku}}. The first recorded case occurred when {{ill|Prince Enshin|ja|延信王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Enshin|1=Nobuzane-ō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q95162004}} (a grandson of {{ill|Emperor Kazan|en|Emperor Kazan|WD=Q361000|lt=Emperor Hanayama}} and a son of {{ill|Prince Kiyohito|ja|清仁親王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Kiyohito|1=Kiyohito-shinnō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17502448}}) was appointed to the post of {{ill|Shingi‐haku|ja|神祇伯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shingi‐haku|1=Minister of Divinities|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17210025}}, the chief administrator of the {{ill|Department of Divinities|en|Department of Divinities|WD=Q2264720|lt=Department of Divinities}} under the ritsuryō system. His appointment set a precedent for his descendants to inherit the position of Shingi‐haku. Although they belonged to the {{ill|Minamoto clan|en|Minamoto clan|WD=Q599881|lt=Hanayama Genji}}, they were originally part of the {{ill|Wang (surname)|en|Wang (surname)|WD=Q804943|lt=Royal Family}}, and up to the early modern period they continued to use the royal title ({{ill|Royal Title|ja|王 (皇族)|lt=Royal Title|lt_ja=王号|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Royal Title|1=ō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q16142365}}) during their tenure as Shingi‐haku, thus preserving a royal aspect in their identity{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|p=142}}. Moreover, the queen performing the left role at the enthronement ceremony of the {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=Emperor}} was customarily chosen from among the daughters (including pseudo‐daughters such as {{ill|Yūshi|ja|猶子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yūshi|1=yūshi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11572068}}) of the Shingi‐haku of the Shirakawa family{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|pp=156-157}}. As a court family, their status was that of a {{ill|Semi‐noble|ja|半家 (公家)|1=Half-house (Kuge)|2=ja|3=半家 (公家)|lt=Semi‐noble|lt_ja=半家|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Semi‐noble|qq=}} , and as kazoku they were a {{ill|Viscount|en|Viscount|WD=Q185902|lt=Viscount}} family{{sfn|小田部雄次|2006|p=332}}. They served as the head family of {{ill|Hakuou Shintō|ja|伯家神道|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hakuou Shintō|1=Hakke Shinto|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11381473}} (also known as the Shirakawa‐ryū Shintō) which oversaw the imperial court rites. Because the office of Shingi‐haku became hereditary, they were also known simply as the “Hakuou” family; furthermore, since it became customary upon assuming the post of Shingi‐haku to revert to royal status, they were also called the “Shirakawa Ōke.” == History == === Establishment of the Shirakawa Hakuou Family === The defining feature of the Shirakawa family was the hereditary succession of the Shingi‐haku office and the adoption of the title {{ill|King|ja|王 (皇族)|lt=Royal Title|lt_ja=王号|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/King|1=ō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q16142365}} upon assuming the post. The Rank of “King” was determined by blood relation to the {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=Emperor}}, and was not inherently linked to an official position{{efn|For details, see {{ill|Imperial Family|ja|皇族|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Family|1=Imperial Family of Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11581068}}.}}. It is a unique phenomenon that a non‐imperial family could perpetuate the royal title. The following explanation of the establishment of the Shirakawa family is offered with this in mind. Prince Enshin was born as the son of {{ill|Prince Kiyohito|ja|清仁親王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Kiyohito|1=Kiyohito-shinnō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17502448}}, who was in turn a son of {{ill|Emperor Hanayama Faho|ja|花山法皇|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Emperor Hanayama Faho|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 花山天皇|1=Emperor Kazan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q361000}}, and in the 2nd year of Manju (1025) he was granted the Minamoto surname and demoted to subject status. However, because his father had been made a pseudo‐son of his grandfather, {{ill|Emperor Reizei|en|Emperor Reizei|WD=Q374125|lt=Emperor Reisen}}, he came to be regarded as part of the Reisen Genji{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|pp=142-143}}. Minamoto Enshin was appointed Shingi‐haku in the 3rd year of Kantoku (1046){{Sfn|赤坂|2020|pp=142-143}}. Enshin’s son, {{ill|Prince Kōshi|ja|康資王|lt=Kōshi|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Kōshi|1=Yasusuke-ō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q95162083}}, was made the adopted son of his grandfather, Prince Kiyohito, and was thus treated as a grandson of Emperor Hanayama; consequently, the Reisen Genji line ended with Enshin{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|p=143}}. Prince Kōshi was appointed Shingi‐haku in the 2nd year of Kōhei (1059){{Sfn|久保田|1975|p=173}}. Although Enshin and Kōshi—father and son—served as Shingi‐haku for two successive generations, at that time no single family had yet monopolized the Shingi‐haku office. After Kōshi, {{ill|Prince Atsusuke|ja|敦輔王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Atsusuke|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (a great‐grandson—treated as a grandson—of {{ill|Emperor Sanjō|en|Emperor Sanjō|WD=Q357231|lt=Emperor Sanjō}}) was appointed Shingi‐haku, and thereafter Shingi‐haku officials were also produced from the {{ill|Murakami Genji|ja|村上源氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami Genji|1=Murakami-Genji|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3867344}}, such as {{ill|Minamoto Genkenchū|ja|源顕仲|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Minamoto Genkenchū|1=Minamoto no Akinaka|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11564368}}, as well as from the {{ill|Ōonakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōonakatomi clan|1=Ōnakatomi clan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11431853}}{{Sfn|久保田|1975|pp=173-174}}. Kōshi’s son, {{ill|Minamoto Genken|ja|源顕康|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Minamoto Genken|1=minamoto no akiyasu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q118746998}}, became the adopted son of {{ill|Minamoto Genkenbō|ja|源顕房|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Minamoto Genkenbō|1=Minamoto no Akifusa|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11564369}} of the Murakami Genji and ascended to Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade with the title {{ill|Shōshinshō|ja|正親正|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōshinshō|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 正親司|1=ookiminotsukasa|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11545651}}. Since the post of Shōshinshō was one typically held by princes, it is possible that Genken later reverted from the Genji to the royal family{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|p=143}}. (However, there is no definitive evidence that Genken was ever appointed Shingi‐haku{{Sfn|久保田|1975|p=175}}.) It was Genken’s son, {{ill|Prince Kenkō|ja|顕広王|lt=Kenkō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Kenkō|1=Prince Kenkō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q22125234}}, who opened the path for the hereditary succession of the Shingi‐haku office. Although Prince Kenkō was a fifth‐generation descendant of {{ill|Emperor Kazan|en|Emperor Kazan|WD=Q361000|lt=Emperor Hanayama}}, as noted above his grandfather, Prince Kōshi, had been made a pseudo‐son of Prince Kiyohito and Prince Kenkō himself was adopted as a pseudo‐son of Kōshi—thus being treated as a third‐generation prince{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|p=144}}. While some sources claim that his reversion to the royal family upon assuming the Shingi‐haku post set a precedent for later generations{{Sfn|曽根|1933|p=31}}, records from the ''Honchō Seiki'' confirm that he was already being called “Prince Kenkō” in his capacity as Shōshinshō before his appointment as Shingi‐haku in the 3rd year of Chōkan (1165){{Sfn|小松|1984|pp=24-27}}. Owing to his superior bloodline among the various princes (with many other lines having grown more distant from the last of Emperor Sanjō’s lineage), Prince Kenkō became the accepted standard of the royal family and effectively established his position as the head of the royal clan{{Efn|Since no head of the royal clan previously existed, the title of royal clan leader ({{ill|Shijaku|ja|氏爵|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shijaku|1=Shijaku|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11547816}}) was customarily held by the first prince; however, at that time, as secularly appointed princes had become rare, this practice had lapsed.}}{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|pp=144-147}}. Moreover, aided by the fact that his younger brother, {{ill|Tendaizashu|ja|天台座主|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tendaizashu|1=Tendai-zasu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11442374}}, who held the post of Great Priest ({{ill|Daishōjō|ja|大僧正|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Daishōjō|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 僧正|1=Sōjō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q15416595}}), had earned the trust of {{ill|Emperor Go‐Shirakawa|ja|後白河法皇|lt=Emperor Go‐Shirakawa|lt_ja=Emperor Go-Shirakawa|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Emperor Go‐Shirakawa|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 後白河天皇|1=Go-Shirakawa|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q317984}}, Prince Kenkō advanced to Lower Fourth Rank and passed the title of Shōshinshō to his eldest son, {{ill|Prince Kengō|ja|顕綱王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Kengō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, and the Shingi‐haku position to his second son, {{ill|Prince Chūshi|ja|仲資王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Chūshi|1=Prince Chūshi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17216452}}{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|pp=148-149}}. Thereafter, his descendants continued to inherit the Shingi‐haku office. This hereditary trend was influenced not only by the general tendency toward hereditary offices from the late Heian period onward but also by the fact that Prince Kōshi’s mother was a granddaughter of {{ill|Ōnakatomi no Sukechika|en|Ōnakatomi no Sukechika|WD=Q3594041|lt=Ōonakatomi Sukechika}} and Genken was a son of the Murakami Genji, indicating close ties with other influential families known for producing Shingi‐haku officials{{Sfn|久保田|1975|pp=175-176}}. === The Branching of the Hanayama Genji === After Prince Kenkō’s retirement, a dispute arose between his two sons, {{ill|Prince Kengō|ja|顕綱王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Kengō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} and {{ill|Prince Chūshi|ja|仲資王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Chūshi|1=Prince Chūshi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17216452}}, over the leadership of the royal clan. In the January conferment ceremony of the 2nd year of {{ill|Jishō|en|Jishō|WD=Q1194671|lt=Jishō}}, both advocated for the conferral of the royal clan title ({{ill|Shijaku|ja|氏爵|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shijaku|1=Shijaku|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11547816}}); the elder, Prince Kengō, argued that his higher Rank entitled him to it, while his younger brother, Prince Chūshi, maintained that the authority to confer the title had been transferred from their father along with the Shingi‐haku office. Although no decision was reached that year and the royal clan title was not conferred, in the autumn of the 3rd year of Jishō (1179) Prince Kengō was recognized as the head of the royal clan, and in the January ceremony of the 4th year of Jishō (1180) the recommendation for the royal title was made by him{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|pp=150-151}}. That it was not Prince Chūshi—the Shingi‐haku—but rather Prince Kengō, who conferred the royal title indicates that at that time the positions of Shingi‐haku and head of the royal clan were not yet linked{{Sfn|小松|1984|pp=38-40}}. Although Prince Kengō subsequently disappears from the records, the defeated Prince Chūshi continued to be promoted, reaching Lower Fourth Rank in the 1st year of {{ill|Genryaku|en|Genryaku|WD=Q1194250|lt=Genryaku}} (1184) and is believed to have become head of the royal clan in that same year{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|p=152}}. After transferring the Shingi‐haku office to his son, {{ill|Prince Gyōshi|ja|業資王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Gyōshi|1=Prince Gyōshi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q95163204}}, Prince Chūshi was promoted to {{ill|Senior Third Rank|lt=Senior Third Rank|lt=Shōsanmi|ja|正三位|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōsanmi|qq=}} and {{ill|Hyōbu‐kyō|ja|兵部卿|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hyōbu‐kyō|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 兵部省|1=Ministry of the Military|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3276048}}, thereby establishing a family status unmatched by any other in terms of the hereditary succession of the Shingi‐haku office and the royal clan{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|pp=154-156}}. The appellation “Shirakawa” began to be used from the time of {{ill|Prince Shihō|ja|白川資邦王|lt=Shihō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Shihō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}—the grandson of Prince Gyōshi—in the mid‑13th century onwardSee, for example, the National History Encyclopedia, Vol. 11 ({{ill|Yoshikawa Kōbunkankān|ja|吉川弘文館|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshikawa Kōbunkankān|1=Yoshikawa Kōbunkan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q4346755}}, 1983 [Shōwa 59]), p. 617.{{Sfn|小松|1984|p=41}}. However, although it was common for court families to be named after their place of residence or villa, any connection between the Shirakawa Hakuou‐ke and the land of {{ill|Shirakawa|ja|白河 (洛外)|lt=Shirakawa|lt_ja=白河|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shirakawa|1=Shirakawa|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11579943}} remains unclear{{Sfn|小松|1984|p=41}}. During the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|en|Nanboku-chō period|WD=Q264012|lt=Nanboku‐chō period}}, the Gyōshi line split into two branches, leading to Shingi‐haku officials emerging from a third branch; however, by the early {{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|WD=Q334845|lt=Muromachi period}}, only the legitimate branch of the Gyōshi line survived as a court family that hereditaryly held the Shingi‐haku office{{Sfn|曽根|1933|pp=33-35}}{{Sfn|久保田|1975|pp=189-193}}{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|pp=158-160}}. At the end of the 15th century, {{ill|Yoshida Kanetomo|en|Yoshida Kanetomo|WD=Q723266|lt=Yoshida Kanku}}, a member of the {{ill|Urabe clan|ja|卜部氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Urabe clan|qq=}} who had long held the post of {{ill|Shingi‐daifu|ja|神祇大副|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shingi‐daifu|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 神祇官|1=Jingi-kan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q2264720}} (the deputy, i.e. the second‐in‐command, of the Jingi‐kan), established {{ill|Yoshida Shintō|en|Yoshida Shintō|WD=Q1760351|lt=Yoshida Shintō}}. By assuming the title of {{ill|Shingi‐kanryō Chōjō|ja|神祇管領長上|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shingi‐kanryō Chōjō|1=Shingi‐kanryō Chōjō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17212391}}, the {{ill|Urabe clan|lt=Urabe clan|lt=Yoshida family|ja|吉田家|1=Urabe clan|2=ja|3=卜部氏|lt=Yoshida family|comment=Might be more of a redirect with potential but this is strictly potential right now|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshida family|qq=}} came to control the majority of shrines nationwide, and the authority of the Shirakawa family declined{{Sfn|曽根|1933|pp=36-37}}. === Disruption of the Male Line Through Adoption Succession === In the 3rd year of {{ill|Eiroku|en|Eiroku|WD=Q1143341|lt=Eirōku}} (1560), when Shingi‐haku Prince Magyō died, his eldest son, Kanchika, was dispatched to {{ill|Tosa Province|en|Tosa Province|WD=Q857330|lt=Tosa Province}}, and his younger brother, Kunitomi, had taken the tonsure. Consequently, the second son of {{ill|Prince Nakaindō Tsuumon|ja|中院通為|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakaindō Tsuumon|1=Nakanoin Michitame|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17226882}} of the Murakami Genji—who was married into the family—was named {{ill|Prince Magahide|ja|白川雅朝王|lt=Magahide|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Magahide|1=Prince Magahide|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q96715018}} and succeeded the Shirakawa family after Prince Magyō’s death{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|p=160}}. Minamoto Magahide was appointed Shingi‐haku in the 12th year of Eirōku (1569) and assumed the royal title as Prince Magahide; later, after renaming himself as Prince Magachō, he passed the Shingi‐haku office to his son, {{ill|Prince Kenshō|ja|白川顕成王|lt=Kenshō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Kenshō|1=Prince Kenshō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q96715124}}, in the 10th year of {{ill|Keichō|en|Keichō|WD=Q1328185|lt=Keichō}} (1605). Upon abdicating as Shingi‐haku, Prince Magachō reverted to the Minamoto name, and from then on the royal title was used only while holding the Shingi‐haku post{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|p=161}}. In addition, while serving as Shingi‐haku he concurrently held the offices of {{ill|Major general|en|Major general|WD=Q157148|lt=Minor General}} and {{ill|Lieutenant general|en|Lieutenant general|WD=Q152951|lt=Middle General}}, establishing a precedent for the Shirakawa family to combine these roles thereafter{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|p=161}}. Moreover, because Prince Magachō’s biological father was a {{ill|Naidaijin|en|Naidaijin|WD=Q1185338|lt=Naidaijin}}, after resigning as Shingi‐haku he became the only member of the Shirakawa family to attain the Rank of {{ill|Sangi (Japan)|en|Sangi (Japan)|WD=Q1133663|lt=Sangi}}{{Sfn|曽根|1933|p=37}}. After the death of Prince Kenshō, the Shirakawa family was succeeded by {{ill|Prince Magachin|ja|白川雅陳王|lt=Magachin|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Magachin|1=Prince Magachin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q96715869}}, who hailed from the Fujiwara‐affiliated {{ill|Takahira Family|ja|高倉家|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takahira Family|1=Takakura family|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11668764}}; from that point onward the Shirakawa Hakuou‐ke ceased to be the direct male‐line descendants of the Emperor. Until Prince Kenshō, the royal title had been conferred along with Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade; however, beginning with Prince Magachin they were enshrined from the outset as Minamoto, only adopting the royal title after their appointment as Shingi‐haku{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|p=162}}. === The Founding of Hakuou Shintō === Although the Shirakawa family later became known as one of the head families of Shintō alongside the Yoshida family, in reality its growing devotion to Shingi‐dō began in the generation of Prince Magayō ({{ill|Prince Magayō|ja|白川雅喬王|lt=Magayō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Magayō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}), the son of Prince Magachin{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|p=163}}. When his son, {{ill|Prince Magakō|ja|白川雅光王|lt=Magakō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Magakō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, appointed {{ill|Usui Masayoshi|ja|臼井雅胤|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Usui Masayoshi|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} as head of studies, Hakuou Shintō was academically systematized; later, by appointing {{ill|Hirata Atsutane|en|Hirata Atsutane|WD=Q2572749|lt=Hirata Atsutami}} as head of studies, it even influenced modern {{ill|State Shinto|en|State Shinto|WD=Q1197248|lt=State Shintō}}{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|p=163}}. {{Main|Hakuou Shintō}} During the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}, the family held the status of {{ill|Semi‐noble|ja|半家 (公家)|1=Half-house (Kuge)|2=ja|3=半家 (公家)|lt=Semi‐noble|lt_ja=半家|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Semi‐noble|qq=}}, and successive heads served as {{ill|Konoe Chūjō|ja|近衛中将|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Konoe Chūjō|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 近衛府|1=Konoefu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11638974}} before becoming Shingi‐haku. In the Edo period the family stipend was 200 koku.{{#tag:ref|According to the “Old Estate Records Database” of the {{ill|National Museum of Japanese History|en|National Museum of Japanese History|WD=Q3330690|lt=National Museum of Japanese History and Folklore}}, during the Bakumatsu period the Manri Kōji domain included: 34 koku 1 to 5 shō 6 gō 9 shaku from Matsuo‐tani in Matsuo‐dani, Katsuno District, Yamashiro Province; 20 koku 7 to 2 shō 9 gō 8 shaku from Matsuro in Katsuno District; 11 koku 1 to 8 shō 8 gō from Kamiyamada in Katsuno District; 50 koku from Shimoueno in Otokun District; 37 koku 7 to from Iwami Kamisato in Otokun District; 8 koku 7 to 5 shō 7 gō from Shimomitsu in Kii District; 31 koku 3 to from Kikkōin in Kii District; and 6 koku 2 to 9 shō 7 gō from Fukakusa in Kii District—totaling 8 villages and 200 koku 1 to 2 shō 8 gō 7 shaku.—Additionally, there were 100 koku allotted for the Shingi territory and shrine expenses.}} === From the Meiji Era Onward === On June 1, in the 2nd year of {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era}} (1869), as part of governmental reforms the then‐incumbent {{ill|Prince Shikun|ja|白川資訓|lt=Shikun|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Shikun|1=Shirakawa Sukenori|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q27920684}} lost his position as Shingi‐haku and, consequently, no longer used the royal title{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|pp=163-164}}. On June 17 of that same year, when the administrative officials merged the court families with the {{ill|Daimyo|en|Daimyo|WD=Q61982|lt=daimyō}} houses to create the {{ill|Kazoku|en|Kazoku|WD=Q241734|lt=Kazoku}} system, the Shirakawa family was classified among the court families as part of the kazoku{{sfn|浅見雅男|1994|p=24}}{{sfn|小田部雄次|2006|p=13-14}}. When the {{ill|Kazoku Edict|ja|華族令|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kazoku Edict|1=Peerage Law|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11620084}} came into effect on July 7 of Meiji 17 (1884), establishing the five‐peerage system—and with no example of a direct appointment to the {{ill|Dainagon|en|Dainagon|WD=Q1354706|lt=Dainagon}} position in the former {{ill|Dōjō Family|ja|堂上家|1=Tōshōke|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Dōjō Family|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11427847}} (a “direct appointment” being one in which one becomes Dainagon without first resigning from the Chūnagon Rank, a practice regarded as a higher honor) (see note{{#tag:ref|group="Note"|The internal regulations for conferral differentiated whether a direct appointment (“nainton”) existed among the successive heads, thereby classifying the Heidō‐jō family as either a count or viscount family.{{sfn|浅見雅男|1994|p=118}}}}—the head of the Shirakawa family, Prince Shikun, was conferred the Rank of {{ill|Viscount|en|Viscount|WD=Q185902|lt=Viscount}}{{sfn|小田部雄次|2006|p=332}}. Prince Shichō, who succeeded Prince Shikun, had no biological children and adopted Hisao, the son of {{ill|Viscount Masao Ueno|ja|上野正雄|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Viscount Masao Ueno|1=Masao Ueno|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11360379}} (himself an illegitimate son of {{ill|Prince Kitashirakawa Yoshihisa|en|Prince Kitashirakawa Yoshihisa|WD=Q3197569|lt=Prince Kitashirakawa Nōku}}), via {{ill|Adoption|en|Adoption|WD=Q180472|lt=adoption}}. However, in 1954 this adoption was dissolved{{Cite book|title=Heisei Shinsyū Kyū Kazoku Kakei Taisei, Vol. I|publisher=Kasumigaoka Kazoku Family Genealogy Editorial Committee|year=1996|access-date=|isbn=4642036709}}, and with the death of Prince Shichō in Shōwa 34 (1959) the Shirakawa family became extinct. == Overview of Shintō According to the “Hakuou‐ka Gakusoku” == * “Shintō is the eternal, unchanging fundamental principle—a great way that holds true in every nation. It is said that Shintō and {{ill|Budō|en|Budō|WD=Q752021|lt=Budo}} (including {{ill|Sumo|en|Sumo|WD=Q40561|lt=Sumo}}) are one, and that the essence of self‐cultivation, family order, and national governance is revealed through the diligent study of imperial classics such as the {{ill|Kojiki|en|Kojiki|WD=Q813031|lt=Kojiki}}, the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|en|Nihon Shoki|WD=Q813935|lt=Nihon Shoki}}, and the {{ill|Kogo Shūi|en|Kogo Shūi|WD=Q531555|lt=Kogo Shūi}}.” == Successive Heads == === Hanayama Royal Line === # {{ill|Prince Enshin|ja|延信王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Enshin|1=Nobuzane-ō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q95162004}} (?-?) – Demoted to subject status as Minamoto Enshin; Extinct in Shōwa 34 (1959) |Family Crest = Japanese Crest Ume.svg |Crest Name = {{ruby|Ume|うめ}} |Main Lineage = {{ill|Genji|ja|源氏#花山源氏|lt=Hanayama Genji|lt_ja=花山源氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Genji|1=Minamoto clan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q599881}} {{ill|Legitimate Line|ja|嫡流|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Legitimate Line|1=Legitimate Line|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11447787}} |Founding Ancestor = {{ill|Minamoto Genken|ja|源顕康|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Minamoto Genken|1=minamoto no akiyasu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q118746998}} |Classification = {{ill|Kuge|en|Kuge|WD=Q1196276|lt=Kuge}} ({{ill|Semi‐noble|ja|半家 (公家)|1=Half-house (Kuge)|2=ja|3=半家 (公家)|lt=Semi‐noble|lt_ja=半家|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Semi‐noble|qq=}})
{{ill|Kazoku|en|Kazoku|WD=Q241734|lt=Kazoku}} ({{ill|Viscount|en|Viscount|WD=Q185902|lt=Viscount}}) |Origin = {{ill|Yamashiro Province|ja|Yamashiro Province|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamashiro Province|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} |Base = {{ill|Yamashiro Province|ja|Yamashiro Province|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamashiro Province|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} |Branch = {{ill|Shinagawa Family (Hanayama Genji)|ja|品川氏#品川氏（花山源氏）|lt=Shinagawa Family|lt_ja=品川氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinagawa Family (Hanayama Genji)|1=Shinagawa Family (Hanayama Genji)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11418409}} ({{ill|Samurai|ja|武家|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Samurai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=buke|WD=Q2927809}}) }} '''Shirakawa Hakuou‐ke''' (白川伯王家), also known as '''Shirakawa‐ke''' (白川家), was a family of Japan’s {{ill|Kuge|en|Kuge|WD=Q1196276|lt=Kuge}} and {{ill|Kazoku|en|Kazoku|WD=Q241734|lt=Kazoku}}. The first recorded case occurred when {{ill|Prince Enshin|ja|延信王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Enshin|1=Nobuzane-ō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q95162004}} (a grandson of {{ill|Emperor Kazan|en|Emperor Kazan|WD=Q361000|lt=Emperor Hanayama}} and a son of {{ill|Prince Kiyohito|ja|清仁親王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Kiyohito|1=Kiyohito-shinnō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17502448}}) was appointed to the post of {{ill|Shingi‐haku|ja|神祇伯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shingi‐haku|1=Minister of Divinities|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17210025}}, the chief administrator of the {{ill|Department of Divinities|en|Department of Divinities|WD=Q2264720|lt=Department of Divinities}} under the ritsuryō system. His appointment set a precedent for his descendants to inherit the position of Shingi‐haku. Although they belonged to the {{ill|Minamoto clan|en|Minamoto clan|WD=Q599881|lt=Hanayama Genji}}, they were originally part of the {{ill|Wang (surname)|en|Wang (surname)|WD=Q804943|lt=Royal Family}}, and up to the early modern period they continued to use the royal title ({{ill|Royal Title|ja|王 (皇族)|lt=Royal Title|lt_ja=王号|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Royal Title|1=ō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q16142365}}) during their tenure as Shingi‐haku, thus preserving a royal aspect in their identity{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|p=142}}. Moreover, the queen performing the left role at the enthronement ceremony of the {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=Emperor}} was customarily chosen from among the daughters (including pseudo‐daughters such as {{ill|Yūshi|ja|猶子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yūshi|1=yūshi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11572068}}) of the Shingi‐haku of the Shirakawa family{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|pp=156-157}}. As a court family, their status was that of a {{ill|Semi‐noble|ja|半家 (公家)|1=Half-house (Kuge)|2=ja|3=半家 (公家)|lt=Semi‐noble|lt_ja=半家|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Semi‐noble|qq=}} , and as kazoku they were a {{ill|Viscount|en|Viscount|WD=Q185902|lt=Viscount}} family{{sfn|小田部雄次|2006|p=332}}. They served as the head family of {{ill|Hakuou Shintō|ja|伯家神道|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hakuou Shintō|1=Hakke Shinto|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11381473}} (also known as the Shirakawa‐ryū Shintō) which oversaw the imperial court rites. Because the office of Shingi‐haku became hereditary, they were also known simply as the “Hakuou” family; furthermore, since it became customary upon assuming the post of Shingi‐haku to revert to royal status, they were also called the “Shirakawa Ōke.” == History == === Establishment of the Shirakawa Hakuou Family === The defining feature of the Shirakawa family was the hereditary succession of the Shingi‐haku office and the adoption of the title {{ill|King|ja|王 (皇族)|lt=Royal Title|lt_ja=王号|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/King|1=ō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q16142365}} upon assuming the post. The Rank of “King” was determined by blood relation to the {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=Emperor}}, and was not inherently linked to an official position{{efn|For details, see {{ill|Imperial Family|ja|皇族|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Family|1=Imperial Family of Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11581068}}.}}. It is a unique phenomenon that a non‐imperial family could perpetuate the royal title. The following explanation of the establishment of the Shirakawa family is offered with this in mind. Prince Enshin was born as the son of {{ill|Prince Kiyohito|ja|清仁親王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Kiyohito|1=Kiyohito-shinnō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17502448}}, who was in turn a son of {{ill|Emperor Hanayama Faho|ja|花山法皇|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Emperor Hanayama Faho|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 花山天皇|1=Emperor Kazan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q361000}}, and in the 2nd year of Manju (1025) he was granted the Minamoto surname and demoted to subject status. However, because his father had been made a pseudo‐son of his grandfather, {{ill|Emperor Reizei|en|Emperor Reizei|WD=Q374125|lt=Emperor Reisen}}, he came to be regarded as part of the Reisen Genji{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|pp=142-143}}. Minamoto Enshin was appointed Shingi‐haku in the 3rd year of Kantoku (1046){{Sfn|赤坂|2020|pp=142-143}}. Enshin’s son, {{ill|Prince Kōshi|ja|康資王|lt=Kōshi|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Kōshi|1=Yasusuke-ō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q95162083}}, was made the adopted son of his grandfather, Prince Kiyohito, and was thus treated as a grandson of Emperor Hanayama; consequently, the Reisen Genji line ended with Enshin{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|p=143}}. Prince Kōshi was appointed Shingi‐haku in the 2nd year of Kōhei (1059){{Sfn|久保田|1975|p=173}}. Although Enshin and Kōshi—father and son—served as Shingi‐haku for two successive generations, at that time no single family had yet monopolized the Shingi‐haku office. After Kōshi, {{ill|Prince Atsusuke|ja|敦輔王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Atsusuke|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (a great‐grandson—treated as a grandson—of {{ill|Emperor Sanjō|en|Emperor Sanjō|WD=Q357231|lt=Emperor Sanjō}}) was appointed Shingi‐haku, and thereafter Shingi‐haku officials were also produced from the {{ill|Murakami Genji|ja|村上源氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami Genji|1=Murakami-Genji|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3867344}}, such as {{ill|Minamoto Genkenchū|ja|源顕仲|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Minamoto Genkenchū|1=Minamoto no Akinaka|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11564368}}, as well as from the {{ill|Ōonakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōonakatomi clan|1=Ōnakatomi clan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11431853}}{{Sfn|久保田|1975|pp=173-174}}. Kōshi’s son, {{ill|Minamoto Genken|ja|源顕康|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Minamoto Genken|1=minamoto no akiyasu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q118746998}}, became the adopted son of {{ill|Minamoto Genkenbō|ja|源顕房|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Minamoto Genkenbō|1=Minamoto no Akifusa|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11564369}} of the Murakami Genji and ascended to Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade with the title {{ill|Shōshinshō|ja|正親正|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōshinshō|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 正親司|1=ookiminotsukasa|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11545651}}. Since the post of Shōshinshō was one typically held by princes, it is possible that Genken later reverted from the Genji to the royal family{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|p=143}}. (However, there is no definitive evidence that Genken was ever appointed Shingi‐haku{{Sfn|久保田|1975|p=175}}.) It was Genken’s son, {{ill|Prince Kenkō|ja|顕広王|lt=Kenkō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Kenkō|1=Prince Kenkō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q22125234}}, who opened the path for the hereditary succession of the Shingi‐haku office. Although Prince Kenkō was a fifth‐generation descendant of {{ill|Emperor Kazan|en|Emperor Kazan|WD=Q361000|lt=Emperor Hanayama}}, as noted above his grandfather, Prince Kōshi, had been made a pseudo‐son of Prince Kiyohito and Prince Kenkō himself was adopted as a pseudo‐son of Kōshi—thus being treated as a third‐generation prince{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|p=144}}. While some sources claim that his reversion to the royal family upon assuming the Shingi‐haku post set a precedent for later generations{{Sfn|曽根|1933|p=31}}, records from the ''Honchō Seiki'' confirm that he was already being called “Prince Kenkō” in his capacity as Shōshinshō before his appointment as Shingi‐haku in the 3rd year of Chōkan (1165){{Sfn|小松|1984|pp=24-27}}. Owing to his superior bloodline among the various princes (with many other lines having grown more distant from the last of Emperor Sanjō’s lineage), Prince Kenkō became the accepted standard of the royal family and effectively established his position as the head of the royal clan{{Efn|Since no head of the royal clan previously existed, the title of royal clan leader ({{ill|Shijaku|ja|氏爵|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shijaku|1=Shijaku|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11547816}}) was customarily held by the first prince; however, at that time, as secularly appointed princes had become rare, this practice had lapsed.}}{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|pp=144-147}}. Moreover, aided by the fact that his younger brother, {{ill|Tendaizashu|ja|天台座主|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tendaizashu|1=Tendai-zasu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11442374}}, who held the post of Great Priest ({{ill|Daishōjō|ja|大僧正|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Daishōjō|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 僧正|1=Sōjō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q15416595}}), had earned the trust of {{ill|Emperor Go‐Shirakawa|ja|後白河法皇|lt=Emperor Go‐Shirakawa|lt_ja=Emperor Go-Shirakawa|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Emperor Go‐Shirakawa|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 後白河天皇|1=Go-Shirakawa|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q317984}}, Prince Kenkō advanced to Lower Fourth Rank and passed the title of Shōshinshō to his eldest son, {{ill|Prince Kengō|ja|顕綱王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Kengō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, and the Shingi‐haku position to his second son, {{ill|Prince Chūshi|ja|仲資王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Chūshi|1=Prince Chūshi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17216452}}{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|pp=148-149}}. Thereafter, his descendants continued to inherit the Shingi‐haku office. This hereditary trend was influenced not only by the general tendency toward hereditary offices from the late Heian period onward but also by the fact that Prince Kōshi’s mother was a granddaughter of {{ill|Ōnakatomi no Sukechika|en|Ōnakatomi no Sukechika|WD=Q3594041|lt=Ōonakatomi Sukechika}} and Genken was a son of the Murakami Genji, indicating close ties with other influential families known for producing Shingi‐haku officials{{Sfn|久保田|1975|pp=175-176}}. === The Branching of the Hanayama Genji === After Prince Kenkō’s retirement, a dispute arose between his two sons, {{ill|Prince Kengō|ja|顕綱王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Kengō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} and {{ill|Prince Chūshi|ja|仲資王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Chūshi|1=Prince Chūshi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17216452}}, over the leadership of the royal clan. In the January conferment ceremony of the 2nd year of {{ill|Jishō|en|Jishō|WD=Q1194671|lt=Jishō}}, both advocated for the conferral of the royal clan title ({{ill|Shijaku|ja|氏爵|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shijaku|1=Shijaku|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11547816}}); the elder, Prince Kengō, argued that his higher Rank entitled him to it, while his younger brother, Prince Chūshi, maintained that the authority to confer the title had been transferred from their father along with the Shingi‐haku office. Although no decision was reached that year and the royal clan title was not conferred, in the autumn of the 3rd year of Jishō (1179) Prince Kengō was recognized as the head of the royal clan, and in the January ceremony of the 4th year of Jishō (1180) the recommendation for the royal title was made by him{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|pp=150-151}}. That it was not Prince Chūshi—the Shingi‐haku—but rather Prince Kengō, who conferred the royal title indicates that at that time the positions of Shingi‐haku and head of the royal clan were not yet linked{{Sfn|小松|1984|pp=38-40}}. Although Prince Kengō subsequently disappears from the records, the defeated Prince Chūshi continued to be promoted, reaching Lower Fourth Rank in the 1st year of {{ill|Genryaku|en|Genryaku|WD=Q1194250|lt=Genryaku}} (1184) and is believed to have become head of the royal clan in that same year{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|p=152}}. After transferring the Shingi‐haku office to his son, {{ill|Prince Gyōshi|ja|業資王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Gyōshi|1=Prince Gyōshi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q95163204}}, Prince Chūshi was promoted to {{ill|Senior Third Rank|lt=Senior Third Rank|lt=Shōsanmi|ja|正三位|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōsanmi|qq=}} and {{ill|Hyōbu‐kyō|ja|兵部卿|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hyōbu‐kyō|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 兵部省|1=Ministry of the Military|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3276048}}, thereby establishing a family status unmatched by any other in terms of the hereditary succession of the Shingi‐haku office and the royal clan{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|pp=154-156}}. The appellation “Shirakawa” began to be used from the time of {{ill|Prince Shihō|ja|白川資邦王|lt=Shihō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Shihō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}—the grandson of Prince Gyōshi—in the mid‑13th century onwardSee, for example, the National History Encyclopedia, Vol. 11 ({{ill|Yoshikawa Kōbunkankān|ja|吉川弘文館|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshikawa Kōbunkankān|1=Yoshikawa Kōbunkan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q4346755}}, 1983 [Shōwa 59]), p. 617.{{Sfn|小松|1984|p=41}}. However, although it was common for court families to be named after their place of residence or villa, any connection between the Shirakawa Hakuou‐ke and the land of {{ill|Shirakawa|ja|白河 (洛外)|lt=Shirakawa|lt_ja=白河|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shirakawa|1=Shirakawa|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11579943}} remains unclear{{Sfn|小松|1984|p=41}}. During the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|en|Nanboku-chō period|WD=Q264012|lt=Nanboku‐chō period}}, the Gyōshi line split into two branches, leading to Shingi‐haku officials emerging from a third branch; however, by the early {{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|WD=Q334845|lt=Muromachi period}}, only the legitimate branch of the Gyōshi line survived as a court family that hereditaryly held the Shingi‐haku office{{Sfn|曽根|1933|pp=33-35}}{{Sfn|久保田|1975|pp=189-193}}{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|pp=158-160}}. At the end of the 15th century, {{ill|Yoshida Kanetomo|en|Yoshida Kanetomo|WD=Q723266|lt=Yoshida Kanku}}, a member of the {{ill|Urabe clan|ja|卜部氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Urabe clan|qq=}} who had long held the post of {{ill|Shingi‐daifu|ja|神祇大副|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shingi‐daifu|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 神祇官|1=Jingi-kan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q2264720}} (the deputy, i.e. the second‐in‐command, of the Jingi‐kan), established {{ill|Yoshida Shintō|en|Yoshida Shintō|WD=Q1760351|lt=Yoshida Shintō}}. By assuming the title of {{ill|Shingi‐kanryō Chōjō|ja|神祇管領長上|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shingi‐kanryō Chōjō|1=Shingi‐kanryō Chōjō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17212391}}, the {{ill|Urabe clan|lt=Urabe clan|lt=Yoshida family|ja|吉田家|1=Urabe clan|2=ja|3=卜部氏|lt=Yoshida family|comment=Might be more of a redirect with potential but this is strictly potential right now|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshida family|qq=}} came to control the majority of shrines nationwide, and the authority of the Shirakawa family declined{{Sfn|曽根|1933|pp=36-37}}. === Disruption of the Male Line Through Adoption Succession === In the 3rd year of {{ill|Eiroku|en|Eiroku|WD=Q1143341|lt=Eirōku}} (1560), when Shingi‐haku Prince Magyō died, his eldest son, Kanchika, was dispatched to {{ill|Tosa Province|en|Tosa Province|WD=Q857330|lt=Tosa Province}}, and his younger brother, Kunitomi, had taken the tonsure. Consequently, the second son of {{ill|Prince Nakaindō Tsuumon|ja|中院通為|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakaindō Tsuumon|1=Nakanoin Michitame|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17226882}} of the Murakami Genji—who was married into the family—was named {{ill|Prince Magahide|ja|白川雅朝王|lt=Magahide|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Magahide|1=Prince Magahide|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q96715018}} and succeeded the Shirakawa family after Prince Magyō’s death{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|p=160}}. Minamoto Magahide was appointed Shingi‐haku in the 12th year of Eirōku (1569) and assumed the royal title as Prince Magahide; later, after renaming himself as Prince Magachō, he passed the Shingi‐haku office to his son, {{ill|Prince Kenshō|ja|白川顕成王|lt=Kenshō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Kenshō|1=Prince Kenshō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q96715124}}, in the 10th year of {{ill|Keichō|en|Keichō|WD=Q1328185|lt=Keichō}} (1605). Upon abdicating as Shingi‐haku, Prince Magachō reverted to the Minamoto name, and from then on the royal title was used only while holding the Shingi‐haku post{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|p=161}}. In addition, while serving as Shingi‐haku he concurrently held the offices of {{ill|Major general|en|Major general|WD=Q157148|lt=Minor General}} and {{ill|Lieutenant general|en|Lieutenant general|WD=Q152951|lt=Middle General}}, establishing a precedent for the Shirakawa family to combine these roles thereafter{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|p=161}}. Moreover, because Prince Magachō’s biological father was a {{ill|Naidaijin|en|Naidaijin|WD=Q1185338|lt=Naidaijin}}, after resigning as Shingi‐haku he became the only member of the Shirakawa family to attain the Rank of {{ill|Sangi (Japan)|en|Sangi (Japan)|WD=Q1133663|lt=Sangi}}{{Sfn|曽根|1933|p=37}}. After the death of Prince Kenshō, the Shirakawa family was succeeded by {{ill|Prince Magachin|ja|白川雅陳王|lt=Magachin|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Magachin|1=Prince Magachin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q96715869}}, who hailed from the Fujiwara‐affiliated {{ill|Takahira Family|ja|高倉家|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takahira Family|1=Takakura family|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11668764}}; from that point onward the Shirakawa Hakuou‐ke ceased to be the direct male‐line descendants of the Emperor. Until Prince Kenshō, the royal title had been conferred along with Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade; however, beginning with Prince Magachin they were enshrined from the outset as Minamoto, only adopting the royal title after their appointment as Shingi‐haku{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|p=162}}. === The Founding of Hakuou Shintō === Although the Shirakawa family later became known as one of the head families of Shintō alongside the Yoshida family, in reality its growing devotion to Shingi‐dō began in the generation of Prince Magayō ({{ill|Prince Magayō|ja|白川雅喬王|lt=Magayō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Magayō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}), the son of Prince Magachin{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|p=163}}. When his son, {{ill|Prince Magakō|ja|白川雅光王|lt=Magakō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Magakō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, appointed {{ill|Usui Masayoshi|ja|臼井雅胤|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Usui Masayoshi|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} as head of studies, Hakuou Shintō was academically systematized; later, by appointing {{ill|Hirata Atsutane|en|Hirata Atsutane|WD=Q2572749|lt=Hirata Atsutami}} as head of studies, it even influenced modern {{ill|State Shinto|en|State Shinto|WD=Q1197248|lt=State Shintō}}{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|p=163}}. {{Main|Hakuou Shintō}} During the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}, the family held the status of {{ill|Semi‐noble|ja|半家 (公家)|1=Half-house (Kuge)|2=ja|3=半家 (公家)|lt=Semi‐noble|lt_ja=半家|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Semi‐noble|qq=}}, and successive heads served as {{ill|Konoe Chūjō|ja|近衛中将|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Konoe Chūjō|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 近衛府|1=Konoefu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11638974}} before becoming Shingi‐haku. In the Edo period the family stipend was 200 koku.{{#tag:ref|According to the “Old Estate Records Database” of the {{ill|National Museum of Japanese History|en|National Museum of Japanese History|WD=Q3330690|lt=National Museum of Japanese History and Folklore}}, during the Bakumatsu period the Manri Kōji domain included: 34 koku 1 to 5 shō 6 gō 9 shaku from Matsuo‐tani in Matsuo‐dani, Katsuno District, Yamashiro Province; 20 koku 7 to 2 shō 9 gō 8 shaku from Matsuro in Katsuno District; 11 koku 1 to 8 shō 8 gō from Kamiyamada in Katsuno District; 50 koku from Shimoueno in Otokun District; 37 koku 7 to from Iwami Kamisato in Otokun District; 8 koku 7 to 5 shō 7 gō from Shimomitsu in Kii District; 31 koku 3 to from Kikkōin in Kii District; and 6 koku 2 to 9 shō 7 gō from Fukakusa in Kii District—totaling 8 villages and 200 koku 1 to 2 shō 8 gō 7 shaku.—Additionally, there were 100 koku allotted for the Shingi territory and shrine expenses.}} === From the Meiji Era Onward === On June 1, in the 2nd year of {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era}} (1869), as part of governmental reforms the then‐incumbent {{ill|Prince Shikun|ja|白川資訓|lt=Shikun|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Shikun|1=Shirakawa Sukenori|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q27920684}} lost his position as Shingi‐haku and, consequently, no longer used the royal title{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|pp=163-164}}. On June 17 of that same year, when the administrative officials merged the court families with the {{ill|Daimyo|en|Daimyo|WD=Q61982|lt=daimyō}} houses to create the {{ill|Kazoku|en|Kazoku|WD=Q241734|lt=Kazoku}} system, the Shirakawa family was classified among the court families as part of the kazoku{{sfn|浅見雅男|1994|p=24}}{{sfn|小田部雄次|2006|p=13-14}}. When the {{ill|Kazoku Edict|ja|華族令|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kazoku Edict|1=Peerage Law|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11620084}} came into effect on July 7 of Meiji 17 (1884), establishing the five‐peerage system—and with no example of a direct appointment to the {{ill|Dainagon|en|Dainagon|WD=Q1354706|lt=Dainagon}} position in the former {{ill|Dōjō Family|ja|堂上家|1=Tōshōke|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Dōjō Family|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11427847}} (a “direct appointment” being one in which one becomes Dainagon without first resigning from the Chūnagon Rank, a practice regarded as a higher honor) (see note{{#tag:ref|group="Note"|The internal regulations for conferral differentiated whether a direct appointment (“nainton”) existed among the successive heads, thereby classifying the Heidō‐jō family as either a count or viscount family.{{sfn|浅見雅男|1994|p=118}}}}—the head of the Shirakawa family, Prince Shikun, was conferred the Rank of {{ill|Viscount|en|Viscount|WD=Q185902|lt=Viscount}}{{sfn|小田部雄次|2006|p=332}}. Prince Shichō, who succeeded Prince Shikun, had no biological children and adopted Hisao, the son of {{ill|Viscount Masao Ueno|ja|上野正雄|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Viscount Masao Ueno|1=Masao Ueno|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11360379}} (himself an illegitimate son of {{ill|Prince Kitashirakawa Yoshihisa|en|Prince Kitashirakawa Yoshihisa|WD=Q3197569|lt=Prince Kitashirakawa Nōku}}), via {{ill|Adoption|en|Adoption|WD=Q180472|lt=adoption}}. However, in 1954 this adoption was dissolved{{Cite book|title=Heisei Shinsyū Kyū Kazoku Kakei Taisei, Vol. I|publisher=Kasumigaoka Kazoku Family Genealogy Editorial Committee|year=1996|access-date=|isbn=4642036709}}, and with the death of Prince Shichō in Shōwa 34 (1959) the Shirakawa family became extinct. == Overview of Shintō According to the “Hakuou‐ka Gakusoku” == * “Shintō is the eternal, unchanging fundamental principle—a great way that holds true in every nation. It is said that Shintō and {{ill|Budō|en|Budō|WD=Q752021|lt=Budo}} (including {{ill|Sumo|en|Sumo|WD=Q40561|lt=Sumo}}) are one, and that the essence of self‐cultivation, family order, and national governance is revealed through the diligent study of imperial classics such as the {{ill|Kojiki|en|Kojiki|WD=Q813031|lt=Kojiki}}, the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|en|Nihon Shoki|WD=Q813935|lt=Nihon Shoki}}, and the {{ill|Kogo Shūi|en|Kogo Shūi|WD=Q531555|lt=Kogo Shūi}}.” == Successive Heads == === Hanayama Royal Line === # {{ill|Prince Enshin|ja|延信王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Enshin|1=Nobuzane-ō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q95162004}} (?-?) – Demoted to subject status as Minamoto Enshin; [[ja:白川伯王家]][[ko:시라카와하쿠오가]][[zh:白川家]] [[ja:白川伯王家]][[ko:시라카와하쿠오가]][[zh:白川家]] [[ja:白川伯王家]][[ko:시라카와하쿠오가]][[zh:白川家]] {{Japanese Clans |Family Name = Shirakawa Family
Extinct in Shōwa 34 (1959) |Family Crest = Japanese Crest Ume.svg |Crest Name = {{ruby|Ume|うめ}} |Main Lineage = {{ill|Genji|ja|源氏#花山源氏|lt=Hanayama Genji|lt_ja=花山源氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Genji|1=Minamoto clan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q599881}} {{ill|Legitimate Line|ja|嫡流|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Legitimate Line|1=Legitimate Line|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11447787}} |Founding Ancestor = {{ill|Minamoto Genken|ja|源顕康|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Minamoto Genken|1=minamoto no akiyasu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q118746998}} |Classification = {{ill|Kuge|en|Kuge|WD=Q1196276|lt=Kuge}} ({{ill|Semi‐noble|ja|半家 (公家)|1=Half-house (Kuge)|2=ja|3=半家 (公家)|lt=Semi‐noble|lt_ja=半家|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Semi‐noble|qq=}})
{{ill|Kazoku|en|Kazoku|WD=Q241734|lt=Kazoku}} ({{ill|Viscount|en|Viscount|WD=Q185902|lt=Viscount}}) |Origin = {{ill|Yamashiro Province|ja|Yamashiro Province|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamashiro Province|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} |Base = {{ill|Yamashiro Province|ja|Yamashiro Province|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamashiro Province|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} |Branch = {{ill|Shinagawa Family (Hanayama Genji)|ja|品川氏#品川氏（花山源氏）|lt=Shinagawa Family|lt_ja=品川氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinagawa Family (Hanayama Genji)|1=Shinagawa Family (Hanayama Genji)|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11418409}} ({{ill|Samurai|ja|武家|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Samurai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=buke|WD=Q2927809}}) }} '''Shirakawa Hakuou‐ke''' (白川伯王家), also known as '''Shirakawa‐ke''' (白川家), was a family of Japan’s {{ill|Kuge|en|Kuge|WD=Q1196276|lt=Kuge}} and {{ill|Kazoku|en|Kazoku|WD=Q241734|lt=Kazoku}}. The first recorded case occurred when {{ill|Prince Enshin|ja|延信王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Enshin|1=Nobuzane-ō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q95162004}} (a grandson of {{ill|Emperor Kazan|en|Emperor Kazan|WD=Q361000|lt=Emperor Hanayama}} and a son of {{ill|Prince Kiyohito|ja|清仁親王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Kiyohito|1=Kiyohito-shinnō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17502448}}) was appointed to the post of {{ill|Shingi‐haku|ja|神祇伯|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shingi‐haku|1=Minister of Divinities|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17210025}}, the chief administrator of the {{ill|Department of Divinities|en|Department of Divinities|WD=Q2264720|lt=Department of Divinities}} under the ritsuryō system. His appointment set a precedent for his descendants to inherit the position of Shingi‐haku. Although they belonged to the {{ill|Minamoto clan|en|Minamoto clan|WD=Q599881|lt=Hanayama Genji}}, they were originally part of the {{ill|Wang (surname)|en|Wang (surname)|WD=Q804943|lt=Royal Family}}, and up to the early modern period they continued to use the royal title ({{ill|Royal Title|ja|王 (皇族)|lt=Royal Title|lt_ja=王号|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Royal Title|1=ō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q16142365}}) during their tenure as Shingi‐haku, thus preserving a royal aspect in their identity{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|p=142}}. Moreover, the queen performing the left role at the enthronement ceremony of the {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=Emperor}} was customarily chosen from among the daughters (including pseudo‐daughters such as {{ill|Yūshi|ja|猶子|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yūshi|1=yūshi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11572068}}) of the Shingi‐haku of the Shirakawa family{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|pp=156-157}}. As a court family, their status was that of a {{ill|Semi‐noble|ja|半家 (公家)|1=Half-house (Kuge)|2=ja|3=半家 (公家)|lt=Semi‐noble|lt_ja=半家|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Semi‐noble|qq=}} , and as kazoku they were a {{ill|Viscount|en|Viscount|WD=Q185902|lt=Viscount}} family{{sfn|小田部雄次|2006|p=332}}. They served as the head family of {{ill|Hakuou Shintō|ja|伯家神道|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hakuou Shintō|1=Hakke Shinto|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11381473}} (also known as the Shirakawa‐ryū Shintō) which oversaw the imperial court rites. Because the office of Shingi‐haku became hereditary, they were also known simply as the “Hakuou” family; furthermore, since it became customary upon assuming the post of Shingi‐haku to revert to royal status, they were also called the “Shirakawa Ōke.” == History == === Establishment of the Shirakawa Hakuou Family === The defining feature of the Shirakawa family was the hereditary succession of the Shingi‐haku office and the adoption of the title {{ill|King|ja|王 (皇族)|lt=Royal Title|lt_ja=王号|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/King|1=ō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q16142365}} upon assuming the post. The Rank of “King” was determined by blood relation to the {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|WD=Q208233|lt=Emperor}}, and was not inherently linked to an official position{{efn|For details, see {{ill|Imperial Family|ja|皇族|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Family|1=Imperial Family of Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11581068}}.}}. It is a unique phenomenon that a non‐imperial family could perpetuate the royal title. The following explanation of the establishment of the Shirakawa family is offered with this in mind. Prince Enshin was born as the son of {{ill|Prince Kiyohito|ja|清仁親王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Kiyohito|1=Kiyohito-shinnō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17502448}}, who was in turn a son of {{ill|Emperor Hanayama Faho|ja|花山法皇|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Emperor Hanayama Faho|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 花山天皇|1=Emperor Kazan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q361000}}, and in the 2nd year of Manju (1025) he was granted the Minamoto surname and demoted to subject status. However, because his father had been made a pseudo‐son of his grandfather, {{ill|Emperor Reizei|en|Emperor Reizei|WD=Q374125|lt=Emperor Reisen}}, he came to be regarded as part of the Reisen Genji{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|pp=142-143}}. Minamoto Enshin was appointed Shingi‐haku in the 3rd year of Kantoku (1046){{Sfn|赤坂|2020|pp=142-143}}. Enshin’s son, {{ill|Prince Kōshi|ja|康資王|lt=Kōshi|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Kōshi|1=Yasusuke-ō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q95162083}}, was made the adopted son of his grandfather, Prince Kiyohito, and was thus treated as a grandson of Emperor Hanayama; consequently, the Reisen Genji line ended with Enshin{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|p=143}}. Prince Kōshi was appointed Shingi‐haku in the 2nd year of Kōhei (1059){{Sfn|久保田|1975|p=173}}. Although Enshin and Kōshi—father and son—served as Shingi‐haku for two successive generations, at that time no single family had yet monopolized the Shingi‐haku office. After Kōshi, {{ill|Prince Atsusuke|ja|敦輔王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Atsusuke|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (a great‐grandson—treated as a grandson—of {{ill|Emperor Sanjō|en|Emperor Sanjō|WD=Q357231|lt=Emperor Sanjō}}) was appointed Shingi‐haku, and thereafter Shingi‐haku officials were also produced from the {{ill|Murakami Genji|ja|村上源氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Murakami Genji|1=Murakami-Genji|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3867344}}, such as {{ill|Minamoto Genkenchū|ja|源顕仲|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Minamoto Genkenchū|1=Minamoto no Akinaka|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11564368}}, as well as from the {{ill|Ōonakatomi clan|ja|大中臣氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ōonakatomi clan|1=Ōnakatomi clan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11431853}}{{Sfn|久保田|1975|pp=173-174}}. Kōshi’s son, {{ill|Minamoto Genken|ja|源顕康|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Minamoto Genken|1=minamoto no akiyasu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q118746998}}, became the adopted son of {{ill|Minamoto Genkenbō|ja|源顕房|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Minamoto Genkenbō|1=Minamoto no Akifusa|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11564369}} of the Murakami Genji and ascended to Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade with the title {{ill|Shōshinshō|ja|正親正|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōshinshō|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 正親司|1=ookiminotsukasa|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11545651}}. Since the post of Shōshinshō was one typically held by princes, it is possible that Genken later reverted from the Genji to the royal family{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|p=143}}. (However, there is no definitive evidence that Genken was ever appointed Shingi‐haku{{Sfn|久保田|1975|p=175}}.) It was Genken’s son, {{ill|Prince Kenkō|ja|顕広王|lt=Kenkō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Kenkō|1=Prince Kenkō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q22125234}}, who opened the path for the hereditary succession of the Shingi‐haku office. Although Prince Kenkō was a fifth‐generation descendant of {{ill|Emperor Kazan|en|Emperor Kazan|WD=Q361000|lt=Emperor Hanayama}}, as noted above his grandfather, Prince Kōshi, had been made a pseudo‐son of Prince Kiyohito and Prince Kenkō himself was adopted as a pseudo‐son of Kōshi—thus being treated as a third‐generation prince{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|p=144}}. While some sources claim that his reversion to the royal family upon assuming the Shingi‐haku post set a precedent for later generations{{Sfn|曽根|1933|p=31}}, records from the ''Honchō Seiki'' confirm that he was already being called “Prince Kenkō” in his capacity as Shōshinshō before his appointment as Shingi‐haku in the 3rd year of Chōkan (1165){{Sfn|小松|1984|pp=24-27}}. Owing to his superior bloodline among the various princes (with many other lines having grown more distant from the last of Emperor Sanjō’s lineage), Prince Kenkō became the accepted standard of the royal family and effectively established his position as the head of the royal clan{{Efn|Since no head of the royal clan previously existed, the title of royal clan leader ({{ill|Shijaku|ja|氏爵|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shijaku|1=Shijaku|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11547816}}) was customarily held by the first prince; however, at that time, as secularly appointed princes had become rare, this practice had lapsed.}}{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|pp=144-147}}. Moreover, aided by the fact that his younger brother, {{ill|Tendaizashu|ja|天台座主|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tendaizashu|1=Tendai-zasu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11442374}}, who held the post of Great Priest ({{ill|Daishōjō|ja|大僧正|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Daishōjō|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 僧正|1=Sōjō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q15416595}}), had earned the trust of {{ill|Emperor Go‐Shirakawa|ja|後白河法皇|lt=Emperor Go‐Shirakawa|lt_ja=Emperor Go-Shirakawa|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Emperor Go‐Shirakawa|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 後白河天皇|1=Go-Shirakawa|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q317984}}, Prince Kenkō advanced to Lower Fourth Rank and passed the title of Shōshinshō to his eldest son, {{ill|Prince Kengō|ja|顕綱王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Kengō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, and the Shingi‐haku position to his second son, {{ill|Prince Chūshi|ja|仲資王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Chūshi|1=Prince Chūshi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17216452}}{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|pp=148-149}}. Thereafter, his descendants continued to inherit the Shingi‐haku office. This hereditary trend was influenced not only by the general tendency toward hereditary offices from the late Heian period onward but also by the fact that Prince Kōshi’s mother was a granddaughter of {{ill|Ōnakatomi no Sukechika|en|Ōnakatomi no Sukechika|WD=Q3594041|lt=Ōonakatomi Sukechika}} and Genken was a son of the Murakami Genji, indicating close ties with other influential families known for producing Shingi‐haku officials{{Sfn|久保田|1975|pp=175-176}}. === The Branching of the Hanayama Genji === After Prince Kenkō’s retirement, a dispute arose between his two sons, {{ill|Prince Kengō|ja|顕綱王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Kengō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} and {{ill|Prince Chūshi|ja|仲資王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Chūshi|1=Prince Chūshi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17216452}}, over the leadership of the royal clan. In the January conferment ceremony of the 2nd year of {{ill|Jishō|en|Jishō|WD=Q1194671|lt=Jishō}}, both advocated for the conferral of the royal clan title ({{ill|Shijaku|ja|氏爵|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shijaku|1=Shijaku|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11547816}}); the elder, Prince Kengō, argued that his higher Rank entitled him to it, while his younger brother, Prince Chūshi, maintained that the authority to confer the title had been transferred from their father along with the Shingi‐haku office. Although no decision was reached that year and the royal clan title was not conferred, in the autumn of the 3rd year of Jishō (1179) Prince Kengō was recognized as the head of the royal clan, and in the January ceremony of the 4th year of Jishō (1180) the recommendation for the royal title was made by him{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|pp=150-151}}. That it was not Prince Chūshi—the Shingi‐haku—but rather Prince Kengō, who conferred the royal title indicates that at that time the positions of Shingi‐haku and head of the royal clan were not yet linked{{Sfn|小松|1984|pp=38-40}}. Although Prince Kengō subsequently disappears from the records, the defeated Prince Chūshi continued to be promoted, reaching Lower Fourth Rank in the 1st year of {{ill|Genryaku|en|Genryaku|WD=Q1194250|lt=Genryaku}} (1184) and is believed to have become head of the royal clan in that same year{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|p=152}}. After transferring the Shingi‐haku office to his son, {{ill|Prince Gyōshi|ja|業資王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Gyōshi|1=Prince Gyōshi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q95163204}}, Prince Chūshi was promoted to {{ill|Senior Third Rank|lt=Senior Third Rank|lt=Shōsanmi|ja|正三位|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shōsanmi|qq=}} and {{ill|Hyōbu‐kyō|ja|兵部卿|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hyōbu‐kyō|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 兵部省|1=Ministry of the Military|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3276048}}, thereby establishing a family status unmatched by any other in terms of the hereditary succession of the Shingi‐haku office and the royal clan{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|pp=154-156}}. The appellation “Shirakawa” began to be used from the time of {{ill|Prince Shihō|ja|白川資邦王|lt=Shihō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Shihō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}—the grandson of Prince Gyōshi—in the mid‑13th century onwardSee, for example, the National History Encyclopedia, Vol. 11 ({{ill|Yoshikawa Kōbunkankān|ja|吉川弘文館|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshikawa Kōbunkankān|1=Yoshikawa Kōbunkan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q4346755}}, 1983 [Shōwa 59]), p. 617.{{Sfn|小松|1984|p=41}}. However, although it was common for court families to be named after their place of residence or villa, any connection between the Shirakawa Hakuou‐ke and the land of {{ill|Shirakawa|ja|白河 (洛外)|lt=Shirakawa|lt_ja=白河|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shirakawa|1=Shirakawa|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11579943}} remains unclear{{Sfn|小松|1984|p=41}}. During the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|en|Nanboku-chō period|WD=Q264012|lt=Nanboku‐chō period}}, the Gyōshi line split into two branches, leading to Shingi‐haku officials emerging from a third branch; however, by the early {{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|WD=Q334845|lt=Muromachi period}}, only the legitimate branch of the Gyōshi line survived as a court family that hereditaryly held the Shingi‐haku office{{Sfn|曽根|1933|pp=33-35}}{{Sfn|久保田|1975|pp=189-193}}{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|pp=158-160}}. At the end of the 15th century, {{ill|Yoshida Kanetomo|en|Yoshida Kanetomo|WD=Q723266|lt=Yoshida Kanku}}, a member of the {{ill|Urabe clan|ja|卜部氏|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Urabe clan|qq=}} who had long held the post of {{ill|Shingi‐daifu|ja|神祇大副|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shingi‐daifu|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 神祇官|1=Jingi-kan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q2264720}} (the deputy, i.e. the second‐in‐command, of the Jingi‐kan), established {{ill|Yoshida Shintō|en|Yoshida Shintō|WD=Q1760351|lt=Yoshida Shintō}}. By assuming the title of {{ill|Shingi‐kanryō Chōjō|ja|神祇管領長上|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shingi‐kanryō Chōjō|1=Shingi‐kanryō Chōjō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17212391}}, the {{ill|Urabe clan|lt=Urabe clan|lt=Yoshida family|ja|吉田家|1=Urabe clan|2=ja|3=卜部氏|lt=Yoshida family|comment=Might be more of a redirect with potential but this is strictly potential right now|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoshida family|qq=}} came to control the majority of shrines nationwide, and the authority of the Shirakawa family declined{{Sfn|曽根|1933|pp=36-37}}. === Disruption of the Male Line Through Adoption Succession === In the 3rd year of {{ill|Eiroku|en|Eiroku|WD=Q1143341|lt=Eirōku}} (1560), when Shingi‐haku Prince Magyō died, his eldest son, Kanchika, was dispatched to {{ill|Tosa Province|en|Tosa Province|WD=Q857330|lt=Tosa Province}}, and his younger brother, Kunitomi, had taken the tonsure. Consequently, the second son of {{ill|Prince Nakaindō Tsuumon|ja|中院通為|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakaindō Tsuumon|1=Nakanoin Michitame|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17226882}} of the Murakami Genji—who was married into the family—was named {{ill|Prince Magahide|ja|白川雅朝王|lt=Magahide|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Magahide|1=Prince Magahide|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q96715018}} and succeeded the Shirakawa family after Prince Magyō’s death{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|p=160}}. Minamoto Magahide was appointed Shingi‐haku in the 12th year of Eirōku (1569) and assumed the royal title as Prince Magahide; later, after renaming himself as Prince Magachō, he passed the Shingi‐haku office to his son, {{ill|Prince Kenshō|ja|白川顕成王|lt=Kenshō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Kenshō|1=Prince Kenshō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q96715124}}, in the 10th year of {{ill|Keichō|en|Keichō|WD=Q1328185|lt=Keichō}} (1605). Upon abdicating as Shingi‐haku, Prince Magachō reverted to the Minamoto name, and from then on the royal title was used only while holding the Shingi‐haku post{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|p=161}}. In addition, while serving as Shingi‐haku he concurrently held the offices of {{ill|Major general|en|Major general|WD=Q157148|lt=Minor General}} and {{ill|Lieutenant general|en|Lieutenant general|WD=Q152951|lt=Middle General}}, establishing a precedent for the Shirakawa family to combine these roles thereafter{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|p=161}}. Moreover, because Prince Magachō’s biological father was a {{ill|Naidaijin|en|Naidaijin|WD=Q1185338|lt=Naidaijin}}, after resigning as Shingi‐haku he became the only member of the Shirakawa family to attain the Rank of {{ill|Sangi (Japan)|en|Sangi (Japan)|WD=Q1133663|lt=Sangi}}{{Sfn|曽根|1933|p=37}}. After the death of Prince Kenshō, the Shirakawa family was succeeded by {{ill|Prince Magachin|ja|白川雅陳王|lt=Magachin|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Magachin|1=Prince Magachin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q96715869}}, who hailed from the Fujiwara‐affiliated {{ill|Takahira Family|ja|高倉家|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takahira Family|1=Takakura family|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11668764}}; from that point onward the Shirakawa Hakuou‐ke ceased to be the direct male‐line descendants of the Emperor. Until Prince Kenshō, the royal title had been conferred along with Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade; however, beginning with Prince Magachin they were enshrined from the outset as Minamoto, only adopting the royal title after their appointment as Shingi‐haku{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|p=162}}. === The Founding of Hakuou Shintō === Although the Shirakawa family later became known as one of the head families of Shintō alongside the Yoshida family, in reality its growing devotion to Shingi‐dō began in the generation of Prince Magayō ({{ill|Prince Magayō|ja|白川雅喬王|lt=Magayō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Magayō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}), the son of Prince Magachin{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|p=163}}. When his son, {{ill|Prince Magakō|ja|白川雅光王|lt=Magakō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Magakō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, appointed {{ill|Usui Masayoshi|ja|臼井雅胤|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Usui Masayoshi|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} as head of studies, Hakuou Shintō was academically systematized; later, by appointing {{ill|Hirata Atsutane|en|Hirata Atsutane|WD=Q2572749|lt=Hirata Atsutami}} as head of studies, it even influenced modern {{ill|State Shinto|en|State Shinto|WD=Q1197248|lt=State Shintō}}{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|p=163}}. {{Main|Hakuou Shintō}} During the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}, the family held the status of {{ill|Semi‐noble|ja|半家 (公家)|1=Half-house (Kuge)|2=ja|3=半家 (公家)|lt=Semi‐noble|lt_ja=半家|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Semi‐noble|qq=}}, and successive heads served as {{ill|Konoe Chūjō|ja|近衛中将|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Konoe Chūjō|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 近衛府|1=Konoefu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11638974}} before becoming Shingi‐haku. In the Edo period the family stipend was 200 koku.{{#tag:ref|According to the “Old Estate Records Database” of the {{ill|National Museum of Japanese History|en|National Museum of Japanese History|WD=Q3330690|lt=National Museum of Japanese History and Folklore}}, during the Bakumatsu period the Manri Kōji domain included: 34 koku 1 to 5 shō 6 gō 9 shaku from Matsuo‐tani in Matsuo‐dani, Katsuno District, Yamashiro Province; 20 koku 7 to 2 shō 9 gō 8 shaku from Matsuro in Katsuno District; 11 koku 1 to 8 shō 8 gō from Kamiyamada in Katsuno District; 50 koku from Shimoueno in Otokun District; 37 koku 7 to from Iwami Kamisato in Otokun District; 8 koku 7 to 5 shō 7 gō from Shimomitsu in Kii District; 31 koku 3 to from Kikkōin in Kii District; and 6 koku 2 to 9 shō 7 gō from Fukakusa in Kii District—totaling 8 villages and 200 koku 1 to 2 shō 8 gō 7 shaku.—Additionally, there were 100 koku allotted for the Shingi territory and shrine expenses.}} === From the Meiji Era Onward === On June 1, in the 2nd year of {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era}} (1869), as part of governmental reforms the then‐incumbent {{ill|Prince Shikun|ja|白川資訓|lt=Shikun|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Shikun|1=Shirakawa Sukenori|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q27920684}} lost his position as Shingi‐haku and, consequently, no longer used the royal title{{Sfn|赤坂|2020|pp=163-164}}. On June 17 of that same year, when the administrative officials merged the court families with the {{ill|Daimyo|en|Daimyo|WD=Q61982|lt=daimyō}} houses to create the {{ill|Kazoku|en|Kazoku|WD=Q241734|lt=Kazoku}} system, the Shirakawa family was classified among the court families as part of the kazoku{{sfn|浅見雅男|1994|p=24}}{{sfn|小田部雄次|2006|p=13-14}}. When the {{ill|Kazoku Edict|ja|華族令|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kazoku Edict|1=Peerage Law|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11620084}} came into effect on July 7 of Meiji 17 (1884), establishing the five‐peerage system—and with no example of a direct appointment to the {{ill|Dainagon|en|Dainagon|WD=Q1354706|lt=Dainagon}} position in the former {{ill|Dōjō Family|ja|堂上家|1=Tōshōke|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Dōjō Family|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11427847}} (a “direct appointment” being one in which one becomes Dainagon without first resigning from the Chūnagon Rank, a practice regarded as a higher honor) (see note{{#tag:ref|group="Note"|The internal regulations for conferral differentiated whether a direct appointment (“nainton”) existed among the successive heads, thereby classifying the Heidō‐jō family as either a count or viscount family.{{sfn|浅見雅男|1994|p=118}}}}—the head of the Shirakawa family, Prince Shikun, was conferred the Rank of {{ill|Viscount|en|Viscount|WD=Q185902|lt=Viscount}}{{sfn|小田部雄次|2006|p=332}}. Prince Shichō, who succeeded Prince Shikun, had no biological children and adopted Hisao, the son of {{ill|Viscount Masao Ueno|ja|上野正雄|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Viscount Masao Ueno|1=Masao Ueno|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11360379}} (himself an illegitimate son of {{ill|Prince Kitashirakawa Yoshihisa|en|Prince Kitashirakawa Yoshihisa|WD=Q3197569|lt=Prince Kitashirakawa Nōku}}), via {{ill|Adoption|en|Adoption|WD=Q180472|lt=adoption}}. However, in 1954 this adoption was dissolved{{Cite book|title=Heisei Shinsyū Kyū Kazoku Kakei Taisei, Vol. I|publisher=Kasumigaoka Kazoku Family Genealogy Editorial Committee|year=1996|access-date=|isbn=4642036709}}, and with the death of Prince Shichō in Shōwa 34 (1959) the Shirakawa family became extinct. == Overview of Shintō According to the “Hakuou‐ka Gakusoku” == * “Shintō is the eternal, unchanging fundamental principle—a great way that holds true in every nation. It is said that Shintō and {{ill|Budō|en|Budō|WD=Q752021|lt=Budo}} (including {{ill|Sumo|en|Sumo|WD=Q40561|lt=Sumo}}) are one, and that the essence of self‐cultivation, family order, and national governance is revealed through the diligent study of imperial classics such as the {{ill|Kojiki|en|Kojiki|WD=Q813031|lt=Kojiki}}, the {{ill|Nihon Shoki|en|Nihon Shoki|WD=Q813935|lt=Nihon Shoki}}, and the {{ill|Kogo Shūi|en|Kogo Shūi|WD=Q531555|lt=Kogo Shūi}}.” == Successive Heads == === Hanayama Royal Line === # {{ill|Prince Enshin|ja|延信王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Enshin|1=Nobuzane-ō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q95162004}} (?-?) – Demoted to subject status as Minamoto Enshin; awarded Senior Fourth Rank, Upper Grade; served as Danjō Daibyaku and as Shingi‐haku. # {{ill|Prince Kōshi|ja|康資王|lt=Kōshi|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Kōshi|1=Yasusuke-ō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q95162083}} (?-1090) – Adopted son of Prince Kiyohito; awarded Junior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade; served as Shingi‐haku and as Ukyō-ken Daifu. # {{ill|Minamoto Genken|ja|源顕康|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Minamoto Genken|1=minamoto no akiyasu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q118746998}} (?-?) – Became the son of Minamoto Genkenbō; attained Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade; held the title Shōshinshō and served as Governor of Aki; possibly reverted to the royal family. # {{ill|Prince Kenkō|ja|白川顕広王|lt=Kenkō|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Kenkō|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 顕広王|1=Prince Kenkō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q22125234}} (1095–1180) – Awarded Senior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade; served as Shingi‐haku. # {{ill|Prince Chūshi|ja|白川仲資王|lt=Chūshi|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Chūshi|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 仲資王|1=Prince Chūshi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17216452}} (1157–1222) – Held the Rank of Shōsanmi;
